title: Understanding Political Participation in Europe: An Integrated Model of Psychosocial and Institutional Factors
content: Contemporary democracies face an apparent paradox: while numerous indicators point to a decline in political trust and democratic functioning, political participation remains relatively stable and is even increasing in some contexts. This study proposes a psychosocial and institutional framework to explain this paradox by jointly analysing political trust, generalized social trust, external political efficacy, and satisfaction with human development as predictors of both institutional and extra-institutional political participation. It also analyses the role of democratic quality as a contextual factor that moderates these relationships. Data from the eleventh wave of the European Social Survey (ESS) were analysed using structural equation modelling and multigroup analysis across countries with varying levels of democratic quality according to the Democracy Index. The results show that generalized social trust and external political efficacy are positively associated with both forms of participation, whereas political trust is positively associated only with institutional participation. All three variables are positively related to satisfaction with human development, which in turn shows a negative association with both forms of participation and acts as a mediating variable. Furthermore, democratic quality moderates these relationships: in flawed democracies, the associations between generalized trust and institutional participation, and between political trust and extra-institutional participation, disappear. Overall, the findings show that political participation depends on the interaction among psychosocial factors, contextual factors, and democratic institutions, integrating insights from political sociology, the social psychology of participation, and relative deprivation theory.
